notesStmt.note: This is one of many similar corrected proof slips of this poem. Horace Traubel includes a facsimile of a nearly identical slip in With Walt Whitman in Camden and notes that although Whitman was in the practice of having poems "set up for private distribution [i.e., to friends and admirers] at the printing office of Henry Curtz," he never gave out the slips until the poems had been published ([Boston: Small, Maynard & Company, 1906] 1:180). As the text of the poem in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891) bears several alterations not present here, this proof slip probably dates to shortly after the poem's first appearance in 1887.
"Shakespere-Bacon's Cipher" was first published in the October 1887 issue of The Cosmopolitan and later included in Good-Bye My Fancy (1891).

lg.head: SHAKSPERE-BACON'S CIPHER.
(A Hint to Scientists.)
lg.l: I doubt it not—then more, far more;
In each old song bequeath'd—in every noble page or text,

In every object, mountain, tree, and star—in every birth and
life,

As part of each—finality of each—meaning, behind the os-
tentostent
,

body.note: From the personal papers of Whitman. Marginal corrections by W.W. himself. These sheets from new poems W. had made for his friend. Traubel
